newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan premier says ready to resign in July.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan premier says ready to resign in July.

text.p: Taiwan Vice President and Premier Lien Chan, under fire over a wave of horrific, unsolved crimes, has said he plans to step down as premier in July.

"Once the National Assembly completes constitutional reforms and starts implementing a new constitution, it's time for me to leave, to resign," Lien Chan told a television call-in show late on Monday. Local newspapers carried his comments on Tuesday.

The once-powerful National Assembly, whose powers have largely shifted to Taiwan's elected parliament, the Legislative Yuan, retains authority to amend the constitution. The body is expected to act on a package of draft amendments by July.

Lien's administration has come under intense and growing criticism over its failure to check or solve a spate of violent crimes, most recently the kidnap, torture and murder of the teenage daughter of a prominent actress.

Lien was expected to propose a modest cabinet reshuffle on Wednesday for approval during the ruling Nationalist Party's central standing committee meeting, but has rejected calls for deeper personnel changes or to step down immediately.
Lien has given no signs of giving up the vice-presidency to which he was elected in 1996. He serves simultaneously as premier, or cabinet chief, at the president's discretion.

Taiwan's parliament on Tuesday narrowly rejected a non-binding resolution that would have urged President Lee Teng-hui to sack Lien, whom Lee has been grooming as his successor, in a bitter row over the ability of Lien's cabinet to fight crime.

The narrow defeat for the opposition-led move against Lee and Lien came minutes after allied opposition politicians used a filibuster to prevent Lee from delivering a keynote address to the largely ceremonial National Assembly.

Anti-government sentiment erupted when police found the body of the 17-year-old daughter of actress Pai Ping-ping floating in a river on April 28. A massive manhunt, complete with late-night checkpoints by heavily armed police, has failed to catch three key suspects.

The crime rekindled anger over police failure to solve the gangland-style murder of a county magistrate and seven others in his home in November and the murder of an opposition leader two weeks later.
More than 50,000 people demonstrated in Taipei on May 4 to demand the resignation of Lien and a cabinet reshuffle. A similar march is planned for Sunday.
Lien said he wanted to take responsibility for the perceived deterioration of law and social order, but felt that political reality prevented him leaving immediately.
"I personally feel this is the government's responsibility, especially my responsibility," Lien said.
Lien said he tendered his resignation in early May but that President Lee Teng-hui declined to accept it.

"The recent situation has caused people unease. It's time for me to consider taking responsibility," the premier said. "But many limits and circumstances prevent me from leaving my current post. That is why I decide to stay on."
Lien said government operations between now and July would be unaffected.

President Lee has apologised for what he called "worsening social law and order", although cabinet officials have issued statistics indicating that despite the high-profile murders, Taiwan's social order has improved.
